docs.title: ICCUB Claude Guide
docs.text:
A practical guide for ICCUB members who have a Claude Pro account and want to use it well: for research, teaching, outreach and day-to-day admin.

  • Getting started

    Your first 30 minutes with a new account, what Pro includes, and what is safe to upload.

  • How to use Claude

    One page per feature: prompting, files, Projects, Artifacts (docs, slides, designs), longer tasks, Research, connectors, email, Chrome, Claude Code, VS Code and Claude Science.

  • Examples

    Short, concrete write-ups by ICCUB members of real tasks, including what went wrong.

  • Contribute

    Share your own example. Anyone at ICCUB can contribute.

docs.title: Contribute
docs.text: Anyone at ICCUB can add an example or improve a page. Short is fine, and failures are as useful as successes.

docs.title: Send an example
docs.text:
1. Download the template: iccub-example-template.md or copy it from the example template page.
  2. Fill it in with any text editor (VS Code, TextEdit, Notepad…). Replace the text in angle brackets. Ten to fifteen minutes is enough.
  3. Email it to vmathieu@ub.edu with the file attached. Add screenshots or other files if they help.

The editors will put it on the site and send you the link.

Not sure how to write it?

Ask Claude: upload the template, describe what you did in a few sentences, and ask "Fill in this template from my description. Keep my wording where you can and ask me about anything missing." Then check the result before you send it.

docs.title: Improve a page
docs.text:
Spotted a mistake, an outdated menu name, or something missing? Email vmathieu@ub.edu with the page link and what to change.

If you use GitHub, you can also open a pull request on the site repository: pages are Markdown files in docs/.

docs.title: Before you send
docs.text:
• Remove anything confidential: unpublished results, student data, passwords, private IP addresses. See Data and privacy.
  • Say whether you want your name on it or prefer to stay anonymous.

docs.title: Conference trip reimbursement from your email
docs.text:
Illustrative example

This example was written by the site editors to show the workflow. It is not yet a real ICCUB experience. If you try it, send us your version and we will replace it.

About this example Author ICCUB Claude Guide editors Date 2026-10-06 Area Admin Tools used Gmail and Google Drive connectors (or Microsoft 365), Claude in Chrome (optional) Time saved About an hour per trip (estimate)

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Back from a conference, gather everything needed for the travel reimbursement: registration receipt, flights, hotel, local transport, per diem dates. Then fill the department's expense sheet and draft the email to the administration, without digging through dozens of emails.

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:
1. Connected the mailbox once (see Email, calendar and documents) and switched on the email and Drive connectors in a new chat.

  2. Gathered the documents:

    I attended a conference in Lisbon from 29 June to 3 July 2026. Search my email for the registration receipt, flight bookings, hotel confirmation, and any other payment related to this trip. Make a table: date, item, supplier, amount, currency, payment method, and a link to the email. Flag anything missing.

    It found five items and flagged that the hotel invoice was a booking confirmation, not an invoice.

  3. Filled the form. Uploaded the department's expense template (Excel) and the list of rules:

    Fill this expense sheet with the items from the table. Use the per diem rules in the attached document for the travel days. Convert any non-euro amounts with the exchange rate on the payment date and say which rate you used.

  4. Drafted the email:

    Draft an email in Catalan to the department administration, attaching the filled sheet, listing the receipts, and asking for the missing hotel invoice procedure. Don't send it.

  5. Checked everything against the receipts, downloaded the attachments, and sent the email myself.

  6. (Optional) For the hotel invoice, used Claude in Chrome to log in to the hotel's booking site and find the invoice download page. I clicked "download" myself.

docs.title: Result
docs.text: All receipts found, an expense sheet filled, and a draft email, in about 15 minutes instead of an hour and a half. One missing document was spotted before submitting rather than after.

docs.title: What to watch for
docs.text:
• Amounts and dates: check every number against the receipts. This is money.
  • Receipts vs. confirmations: administration usually needs invoices. Ask Claude to flag the difference.
  • Attachments: connectors can read attachments, but writing tools may not be able to attach files to emails. Attach them yourself.
  • Don't let it send. Ask for drafts.
  • Personal data: your mailbox has other people's data. Keep the search specific to the trip.
  • UB rules change: give it the current rules document rather than relying on what it "knows".

docs.title: Organise a seminar series
docs.text:
Illustrative example

This example was written by the site editors to show the workflow. It is not yet a real ICCUB experience. If you try it, send us your version and we will replace it.

About this example Author ICCUB Claude Guide editors Date 2026-10-06 Area Admin Tools used A Project, Gmail and Google Calendar connectors Time saved A few hours per term (estimate)

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Run the term's group seminar series: invite speakers, find dates, send announcements, and keep a schedule, with less back-and-forth email.

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:
1. Created a Project "Seminars 2026–27" with the list of possible speakers, the room booking rules, and last year's announcement emails as style examples. Instructions: "Announcements in English, short, with title, abstract, speaker, date, room 503, and Zoom link placeholder."

  2. Found dates, with the calendar connector:

    Find all Wednesdays at 12:00 between 14 October and 16 December when I have nothing in my calendar. Exclude the week of 2 November.

  3. Drafted invitations, one per speaker, adapted to each: "Draft an invitation to each speaker on the list, proposing two of the free dates, mentioning their recent paper on arXiv if you can find it." Sent them myself after reading.

  4. Tracked replies: later, "Check my email for replies to the seminar invitations and update the schedule table. Who hasn't answered?"

  5. Created calendar events and announcements once a speaker confirmed: "Create the calendar event and draft the announcement for the ICCUB mailing list from their title and abstract in their email."

docs.title: Result
docs.text: A full term's schedule set up in two short sessions, consistent announcements, and a table showing who still needed a reminder.

docs.title: What to watch for
docs.text:
• Check the speaker information (affiliation, title, paper) before it goes into an announcement.
  • Calendar actions: Claude asks before creating events. Read the date, time and time zone carefully, especially for remote speakers.
  • Send invitations yourself. A personal note from you works better than a perfect template.

docs.title: An animated web page for a public event
docs.text:
Illustrative example

This example was written by the site editors to show the workflow. It is not yet a real ICCUB experience. If you try it, send us your version and we will replace it.

About this example Author ICCUB Claude Guide editors Date 2026-10-06 Area Outreach Tools used claude.ai Artifacts, then Claude Code for the final version Time saved Days of web development, for someone who doesn't build websites (estimate)

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: For an open day stand, make an interactive page that visitors can play with on a tablet: "Build a solar system", where you place planets around a star and watch the orbits, with a short explanation of Kepler's laws. No web development skills needed.

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:
1. Described it in a chat, asking for an Artifact:

    Make an interactive web page for a science fair, for visitors aged 10 and up. A star in the centre; visitors tap to add planets at different distances; planets orbit with realistic Kepler speeds (inner ones faster). Show each planet's orbital period. A "Explain" button opens a three-sentence explanation of Kepler's third law. Big buttons, works on a tablet, colourful but not childish. Text in Catalan, Spanish and English with a language switch.

  2. Iterated by playing with it, in the same chat:

    Planets are too small on a tablet. Add trails behind the planets. Add a "reset" button. When two planets are too close, show a warning "Unstable orbit!".

  3. Checked the physics: "Show me the formula you use for the period and the units." Verified that doubling the distance gives a period × 2.83.

  4. Published it with the Artifact's Publish button to get a link and a QR code for the stand. For a permanent version on the ICCUB website, downloaded the HTML file and gave it to the web team.

docs.title: Result
docs.text: A working, bilingual, touch-friendly page in about an hour, used on a tablet at the stand. Children played with it; parents read the explanation.

docs.title: What to watch for
docs.text:
• Physics shortcuts: animations often fake the physics (circular orbits, wrong speed ratios). Ask what is computed and check.
  • Translations: have a native speaker check the Catalan and Spanish texts.
  • Published Artifacts are public: anyone with the link can see them. Nothing confidential in them.
  • Test on the real device before the event: tablets differ in screen size and touch behaviour.
  • For something bigger (several pages, maintained over years), use Claude Code on a proper repository instead of an Artifact.

docs.title: Prepare a public talk from a research paper
docs.text:
Illustrative example

This example was written by the site editors to show the workflow. It is not yet a real ICCUB experience. If you try it, send us your version and we will replace it.

About this example Author ICCUB Claude Guide editors Date 2026-10-06 Area Outreach Tools used claude.ai chat with file upload, Artifacts Time saved About half a day (estimate)

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Give a 30-minute talk at a cultural centre ("Pint of Science" style) about our recent paper on gravitational waves, for an adult audience with no science background.

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:
1. Uploaded the paper and described the audience:

    I'll give a 30-minute talk about this paper to adults with no science background, in a bar, in Catalan. Propose a storyline: an opening hook, three key ideas maximum, and an ending that people remember. No equations.

  2. Asked for analogies and checked them:

    Give me five everyday analogies for how a gravitational-wave detector works. For each, say where the analogy breaks down.

    Kept two; discarded the ones that were misleading.

  3. Built the slide plan: "Turn the storyline into 15 slides: title, one sentence of text maximum, and what image to show." Made the slides myself in our usual software with real images (ESA/NASA/LIGO public images, credited).

  4. Prepared for questions: "What are the ten questions a curious non-specialist is most likely to ask after this talk? Draft a short, honest answer to each."

  5. Rehearsed by pasting my spoken script and asking: "Where would a non-specialist get lost? Which sentences are too long to say out loud?"

docs.title: Result
docs.text: A clear storyline, a slide plan, two good analogies, and a list of likely questions. The talk itself, the images and the delivery remained mine.

docs.title: What to watch for
docs.text:
• Analogies can mislead. Always ask where they break down.
  • Simplification vs. error: check that simplified statements are still true.
  • Images: Claude can't provide usable images; use public agency images with credits, or your own.
  • Don't let it sound generic. Add your own stories: why you work on this, what surprised you.

docs.title: Research examples
docs.text:
• Write a conference proceeding: slides, analysis note and the conference template in one folder, one long prompt, and a finished proceeding in about half an hour.
  • Speed up the code behind a published paper: hand-written Monte Carlo code reviewed by Claude, Antigravity and a local model, now more than 10 times faster.
  • Run a local LLM on your laptop: install Ollama, pick a model that fits your RAM, and use it from the terminal and VS Code.
  • Share a local LLM over the network: serve models from one Mac to another on the same network, including a working VS Code coding agent.
  • A weekly arXiv digest: a scheduled task that checks INSPIRE every Monday morning for new papers citing your work and on your topics.

docs.title: Speed up the code behind a published paper
docs.text: About this example Author Vincent Mathieu Date 2026-10-09 Area Hadron physics (theory) Tools used Claude Code, Google Antigravity (Gemini) and a local model, each given access to the code folder Time saved Review done in about half an hour; the code now runs more than 10 times faster Paper High-energy η(′)π photoproduction and the nature of exotic waves, G. Montaña, V. Mathieu et al., Phys. Lett. B 872 (2026) 140101 (arXiv:2510.14549)

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
In 2025 we published a paper with Gloria Montaña and colleagues on high-energy ηπ production. The model has five variables, and computing the observables meant integrating over four of them.

I wrote the Monte Carlo code myself, fairly quickly, partly while travelling. I deliberately used no libraries: I wanted to understand every step, so every routine was written by hand, from the Monte Carlo integration to the determinant of a 6×6 matrix used to check the boundaries of the physical region. It worked, and it was used for the paper, but a full run took hours.

A year later, when I started using AI coding tools, I wanted to know whether this code could be made faster.

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:
1. Gave the tool access to the folder with the code that produced the published results.
  2. Explained the context: the paper, and that this was the code used for it.
  3. Asked for a review, in substance: "This is the code that was used to publish this paper. Look at all the files and check whether we can optimise it."
  4. Repeated the exercise with three tools: Google Antigravity (with Gemini), Claude (Sonnet, in Claude Code) and a local model, to see whether they would reach the same conclusions.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
The review took about half an hour. It found:

  • Duplicated work: several places where the same quantity was computed twice, each worth a factor of 2.
  • Inefficient routines: my hand-written determinant routine was not efficient.

Together these gave a speed-up of more than a factor of 10. A year after the paper, the same code runs much, much faster.

All three tools (Antigravity, Claude and the local model) led to the same conclusion: the code became much more efficient after the AI review.

docs.title: What to watch for
docs.text:
• Write it yourself first. I think it is a good idea to start by coding every function yourself, without libraries, so that you understand both the physics and the code.
  • Then optimise with AI. Once the code works and has been checked, and you need it efficient to produce the real numbers, ask an AI to optimise it. You keep the understanding and get efficient code.
  • Check the results are unchanged. Compare the optimised code's output with the published numbers before using it.
  • Any tool will do. Here a cloud tool and a local model found the same improvements; if your code cannot leave your machine, see Run a local LLM on your laptop.

docs.title: Write a conference proceeding
docs.text: About this example Author Vincent Mathieu Date 2026-09-28 Area Hadron physics (theory) Tools used Claude with access to a local project folder Time saved The proceeding was written in about half an hour Result Meson photoproduction at Jefferson Lab: from two-meson final states to meson-baryon spin-density matrices (INSPIRE)

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
Two months earlier I had given a plenary talk at the MESON conference in Kraków. I usually don't write proceedings, but this time my experimental colleagues from the GlueX collaboration needed one. They had used formulas I derived that are not yet published, because the paper is not finished. A PhD student who did the analysis wanted to present his preliminary results in a proceeding of his own, and he needed a reference for the formalism. So they asked me to write a proceeding they could cite.

The request came on Slack while I was at another conference, listening to talks. I had no time to write it myself.

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:
1. Created a new folder for the proceeding and put in it:

    • the slides of my MESON talk,
    • my analysis note, the one I will later use to write the full paper,
    • the LaTeX template downloaded from the conference website.

  2. Gave Claude access to everything in the folder.

  3. Wrote one long prompt telling Claude the whole story:

    • I gave a plenary talk at this conference, with the link to the conference website.
    • The slides are the content of the talk, and the analysis note contains the formalism.
    • Why the proceeding is needed: my GlueX colleagues and their PhD student must be able to cite the formalism before the paper is out.
    • The proceeding must follow the conference template.

  4. Read the draft. About half an hour later the proceeding was written.

  5. Finished it by hand:

    • removed one sentence that was not appropriate,
    • added my email and my grant numbers,
    • submitted it to arXiv and to the conference proceedings.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
The proceeding was clear, concise, exactly what I wanted, and formatted the way the conference required. Apart from the one sentence I removed, I kept the text as Claude wrote it.

It is on arXiv and INSPIRE: Meson photoproduction at Jefferson Lab: from two-meson final states to meson-baryon spin-density matrices. My colleagues can now cite the formalism in their own proceeding.

docs.title: What to watch for
docs.text:
• Give the full context. The long prompt with the whole story (who needs it, why, and what it must contain) is what made the first draft usable.
  • Put the real sources in the folder. Slides, analysis note and the official template meant Claude worked from my material rather than from general knowledge.
  • Read every sentence. One sentence was not appropriate and had to go. You remain the author.
  • Unpublished work. The analysis note contained results that are not yet published. Check what you are allowed to share before you give Claude access. See Data and privacy.
  • The details are yours to add: author email, affiliations, grant numbers, acknowledgements.

docs.title: Run a local LLM on your laptop
docs.text: About this example Author Vincent Mathieu Date to confirm Tools used Ollama, Gemma 2, Hermes Agent, VS Code with the Continue extension Why local Data never leaves your machine, no token costs, works offline

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Run an open-weight language model entirely on a personal laptop, use it as a chat assistant in the terminal, and plug it into VS Code as a coding assistant, so that sensitive code and data never go to a cloud service.

docs.title: 1. Pick a model that fits your RAM
docs.text:
Open-weight models come in sizes measured in billions of parameters (2B, 8B, 27B). They are usually distributed 4-bit quantized (Q4), which cuts memory needs a lot with little loss in quality.

Laptop RAM Recommended models Command Good for 8 GB Gemma 2 2B, Phi-3 Mini 3.8B ollama run gemma2:2b Quick chat, code snippets, offline drafting 16 GB Gemma 2 9B, Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 7B ollama run gemma2:9b The sweet spot: reasoning, coding help, analysis 32 GB or more Gemma 2 27B, Qwen 2.5 14B or 32B ollama run gemma2:27b Harder reasoning, larger refactors, agent tasks

docs.title: 2. Install Ollama
docs.text:
Ollama runs in the background, downloads models and serves them through a local API on http://localhost:11434.

  • macOS: download from ollama.com/download, or brew install ollama
  • Windows: download and run OllamaSetup.exe from ollama.com/download
  • Linux: curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh

Essential commands:

ollama run gemma2:9b   # download the model if needed and start a chat
ollama list            # models stored on this machine
ollama ps              # model currently loaded in memory
ollama rm gemma2:9b    # delete a model to free disk space

docs.title: 3. Optional: a terminal agent (Hermes Agent)
docs.text:
ollama run gives a plain chatbot. An agent harness such as Hermes Agent turns the terminal into a workspace where the model can read and run files and call tools.

  1. On first launch, Hermes asks which inference backend to use: choose Ollama.
  2. It detects the models you have pulled (for example gemma2:9b) on localhost:11434.
hermes agent --model gemma2:9b

docs.title: 4. VS Code with the Continue extension
docs.text:
1. Open the Extensions tab (Cmd+Shift+X or Ctrl+Shift+X).
  2. Install Continue.
  3. Continue detects Ollama on localhost:11434 and lists your models. To set one explicitly, add to its config:
{ "models": [ { "title": "Local Gemma 2 (9B)", "provider": "ollama", "model": "gemma2:9b" } ] }

Shortcuts: Cmd+L / Ctrl+L opens the chat about your open files; Cmd+I / Ctrl+I edits selected code inline; Tab accepts completions.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
A working local assistant in the terminal and in VS Code. Two quick tests that worked:

  • In the terminal: ollama run gemma2:9b, then "Write a Python function to validate email addresses using regex."
  • In VS Code: select a block of code, press Cmd+I, and ask "Add docstrings, type annotations, and handle potential ZeroDivisionError." Review the diff, then accept.

docs.title: What to watch for
docs.text:
• Fan noise or slow answers: run ollama ps. On 8 or 16 GB machines, make sure only one large model is loaded. Ollama unloads idle models after about 5 minutes.
  • Quality: small local models are well behind Claude on hard reasoning. Use them where privacy or offline use matters, not as a drop-in replacement.

Next step: share one machine's models with colleagues over the network.

docs.title: Share a local LLM over the network
docs.text: About this example Author Vincent Mathieu Date 2026-09-26 Tools used Ollama, LM Studio, VS Code with the Continue extension Setup A newer MacBook Pro as server, an older MacBook Pro as client, same local network

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
Check that local models running on one Mac (the server) can be used from a second Mac (the client) on the same network, both as a chat model and as a coding agent in VS Code. This is a proof of concept for one shared workstation serving several researchers, with no cloud API costs and no data leaving the local network.

Models on the server: qwen3-coder:30b, qwen2.5-coder:7b, gemma4:e4b, gemma4:e2b, gemma4:12b-mlx.

docs.title: 1. Server: expose Ollama and LM Studio on the network
docs.text:
Find the server's IP address:

ipconfig getifaddr en0

Ollama only listens on localhost by default. Make it listen on the network:

launchctl setenv OLLAMA_HOST "0.0.0.0:11434"

Quit Ollama completely and start it again, then check that it lists your models:

curl http://localhost:11434/api/tags

For LM Studio: Developer (Server) tab, load a model, start the server, and set it to serve on the local network rather than 127.0.0.1. The default port is 1234.

docs.title: 2. Server: firewall
docs.text: In System Settings, Network, Firewall: if the firewall is on, accept the incoming-connection prompts for Ollama and LM Studio the first time a client connects, or add them under Firewall Options.

docs.title: 3. Client: check the connection and chat from the terminal
docs.text:
Replace <server-ip> with the server's address:

ping <server-ip>
curl http://<server-ip>:11434/api/tags
curl http://<server-ip>:1234/v1/models

Chat with a model running on the server (the client needs Ollama installed but no models):

OLLAMA_HOST=http://<server-ip>:11434 ollama run qwen3-coder:30b

This was the first proof that remote access works.

docs.title: 4. Client: VS Code with the Continue extension
docs.text:
1. Install Continue (the open-source AI code agent) in VS Code.
  2. Also install the YAML extension by Red Hat. Without it, Continue silently fails to read its config.
  3. Back up any existing ~/.continue/config.yaml, then write:
name: Remote LAN Models
version: 1.0.0
schema: v1

models:
  - name: "Qwen3 Coder 30B (remote)"
    provider: ollama
    model: qwen3-coder:30b
    apiBase: http://<server-ip>:11434
    roles: [chat, edit, apply]
    capabilities: [tool_use]
    defaultCompletionOptions:
      contextLength: 32768

  - name: "Qwen2.5 Coder 7B (remote, faster)"
    provider: ollama
    model: qwen2.5-coder:7b
    apiBase: http://<server-ip>:11434
    roles: [chat, edit, apply]
    capabilities: [tool_use]

  - name: "Gemma4 e4b (remote, general)"
    provider: ollama
    model: gemma4:e4b
    apiBase: http://<server-ip>:11434
    roles: [chat]
  1. Run Cmd+Shift+P, then Developer: Reload Window.
  2. Open the Continue panel, pick a model, and send a test message.

docs.title: 5. Tests
docs.text:
From an empty folder, in Continue's Agent mode:

  1. Connection check: "What model are you and what's 17 × 24?"
  2. Tool use: "Create a file called hello.py in this folder that prints 'Hello from the remote model' and then run it."
  3. Multi-step edit: "Add a function to hello.py that computes the Fibonacci sequence up to n=10, then run it again."

docs.title: Result
docs.text: Working end to end: terminal chat and VS Code Agent mode both ran against the remote model, and hello.py was created and run by it. Noticeably slower than running locally, especially with the 30B model, but correct.

docs.title: What to watch for
docs.text:
• Agent mode prints tool calls instead of running them: a known Continue bug with provider: ollama in Agent and Plan modes (plain chat is fine). Switch that model to provider: openai, with apiBase: http://<server-ip>:11434/v1 and a placeholder apiKey: "ollama".
  • Config silently ignored: install the Red Hat YAML extension.
  • Speed: the 30B model is slow over the network. Use the 7B model when responsiveness matters.
  • IP address changes: give the server a fixed IP or a .local hostname before several people depend on it, or every client config breaks when the address changes.

docs.title: Demo tips
docs.text: Show the terminal chat first (simplest), then the VS Code file-creation test, which is the more convincing "real coding agent" moment. Pick the 7B model if the demo needs to feel fast, or explain the trade-off: privacy and no cost against speed.

docs.title: A weekly arXiv digest, delivered every Monday
docs.text: About this example Author Vincent Mathieu Date 2026-10-12 Area Hadron physics (theory) Tools used A Claude scheduled task, the public INSPIRE-HEP API Time saved The Monday scan of new papers, every week

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
Every week dozens of papers appear in hep-ph, nucl-th and hep-lat. I wanted one short list on Monday morning with two things: the new papers that cite my work, and the new papers on my own topics (Regge theory, photoproduction, amplitude analysis, exotic hadrons, glueballs, sum rules, lattice spectroscopy), each with one or two sentences on why it matters to me.

Instead of asking Claude for this every week, I wrote the request once and made it a scheduled task: Claude runs the same prompt by itself at a fixed time and leaves the result for me to read.

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:
1. Chose the source. INSPIRE-HEP has a free public API that needs no login. It knows who cites whom, which arXiv listings alone do not. I identify myself with my INSPIRE author ID (V.Mathieu.1, shown on your INSPIRE author page).

  2. Wrote the queries as complete URLs. One for citations of my work, three for my topics. Each URL is written out in full in the prompt (see the warning below on why).

  3. Wrote the prompt. It says who I am, what to fetch, what to keep, and what the digest must look like. A shortened version you can adapt:

    This is an automated run of a scheduled task. The user is not present to
answer questions. Do not ask clarifying questions, do not take any "write"
actions; if in doubt, report what you found.

You are producing a weekly literature digest for <your name>, working on
<your topics>, INSPIRE author ID "<your ID>", mostly in arXiv categories
<your categories>.

Use the INSPIRE-HEP public API. Fetch each URL below exactly as written.

Step 1, papers citing my work. Fetch:
https://inspirehep.net/api/literature?sort=mostrecent&size=25&q=refersto:a%20<your ID>&fields=titles,abstracts,arxiv_eprints,authors,earliest_date
Keep only entries whose earliest_date is in the last 7 days.
If this query fails, say so instead of reporting "no citations".

Step 2, new papers on my topics. Fetch:
https://inspirehep.net/api/literature?sort=mostrecent&size=20&q=(t%20<topic 1>%20or%20t%20<topic 2>)&fields=titles,abstracts,arxiv_eprints,authors,earliest_date
(one URL per group of topics)
Keep the last 7 days, aim for 10 to 15 papers, favour close matches.

Step 3, remove duplicates between steps 1 and 2.

Step 4, present two sections: "Papers citing your work" and "New papers
on your topics". For each paper: title, first author (et al. if more
than 3), arXiv link, and 1 to 2 sentences on why it is relevant to me.
Keep it short and scannable.

  4. Ran it once by hand and checked the result against INSPIRE before scheduling anything.

  5. Scheduled it: every Monday at 08:00, Madrid time. You can ask Claude directly, "Make this a scheduled task that runs every Monday at 8:00", and it shows up in your list of scheduled tasks, where you can pause, edit or run it on demand.

docs.title: Result
docs.text: On Monday I open the run and find the digest. This week it listed eleven papers citing my work, among them a reanalysis of the X(2370) in J/ψ radiative decays and a lattice study of fully charmed tetraquarks, each with an arXiv link and a two-line summary. It also said plainly that none of the topic queries had anything newer than September, so I knew the section was empty, not broken.

docs.title: What to watch for
docs.text:
• Nobody is there to click "Allow". A scheduled task runs while you are away. The first automatic run of this one failed: every web request needed a permission I was not there to give, and Claude reported that it had no papers instead of inventing some. Run the task once by hand, accept the permissions it asks for, and check the next automatic run.
  • Write the URLs in full. The web fetch tool only opens URLs that appear exactly in the prompt, so Claude cannot build a query from a template at run time. Very long URLs are also refused, so split long topic lists into several short queries.
  • Ask it to report failures. "If this query fails, say so" turns a silent empty section into a clear message.
  • Check what it summarises. Results pass through a summariser, and a few "citing" papers turned out unrelated (nuclear PDFs, accelerator software). Open INSPIRE before you cite anything.
  • One run, one report. Ask for a chat message, not a file, and no "write" actions: an unattended task should read and report, not change things for you.
  • It uses your Pro allowance. Each run counts like a normal conversation. Weekly is cheap; every hour is not.

docs.text:

docs.title: Exercise sheets with solutions, in a Project
docs.text:
Illustrative example

This example was written by the site editors to show the workflow. It is not yet a real ICCUB experience. If you try it, send us your version and we will replace it.

About this example Author ICCUB Claude Guide editors Date 2026-10-06 Area Teaching Tools used claude.ai Projects, extended thinking Time saved About 2 hours per sheet (estimate)

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Produce weekly problem sheets for a course, at the right level, with full solutions for the teaching assistants, and without repeating last year's problems.

docs.title: What I did
docs.text:
1. Created a Project "Electromagnetism, problem sheets" and uploaded: the syllabus, the lecture notes, last year's sheets and exams (so it can avoid repeating them).

  2. Project instructions:

    Course: Electromagnetism, 2nd year Physics, UB. Problem sheets in Catalan.
Each sheet: 5 problems, increasing difficulty, covering only material taught up to that week.
Format: LaTeX, using the exam class. Solutions in a separate file.
Don't reuse problems from the uploaded past sheets and exams.
Solutions must be complete, with every step, and a final numerical check.

  3. Each week, with extended thinking on:

    Week 6 covered Gauss's law in matter and boundary conditions (lecture notes ch. 6). Make the sheet and the solutions.

  4. Checked the solutions by asking for an independent check in a new chat (so it doesn't just agree with itself):

    Here is a problem and a proposed solution. Solve it independently, then compare and point out any error.

  5. Corrected by hand and compiled.

docs.title: Result
docs.text: A sheet and a solutions file each week, in about 30 minutes of review instead of 2 to 3 hours of writing.

docs.title: What to watch for
docs.text:
• Solutions contain errors surprisingly often on harder problems: units, signs, a wrong limit. The independent re-check catches some; you must catch the rest.
  • Problems can be unsolvable as stated (missing data, inconsistent numbers). Solve them yourself or have a TA do it before publishing.
  • Originality: problems may resemble well-known textbook ones. That is usually fine for practice, less so for exams.

docs.title: Turn your slides into lecture notes, chapter by chapter
docs.text: About this example Author Vincent Mathieu Date 2026-10-08 Area Teaching (university course) Tools used Claude with access to a local folder, LaTeX Result Lecture notes in Catalan and Spanish, published on the UB Campus Virtual

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Write proper lecture notes for my course from my lecture slides, in both languages the course is taught in (Catalan and Spanish), and publish them for students on the UB Campus Virtual.

docs.title: 1. Put everything in one folder
docs.text:
I opened Claude, created a new folder, and put in it:

  • the slides of my lectures,
  • references: some books I had,
  • the pla docent (the official course teaching plan).

The more context you give, the better and more refined the result.

docs.title: 2. Build the template first
docs.text:
Before writing any content, we created a LaTeX template together, with the style I wanted: fonts, colours, layout, everything. I only moved on once I was happy with the template.

It also works well to give the structure yourself: draft the LaTeX skeleton with the chapters and sections you want, and Claude fills it in.

docs.title: 3. Write chapter by chapter
docs.text: I then asked Claude to write the lecture notes chapter by chapter, based on my slides and following the pla docent.

docs.title: 4. Review by writing comments directly in the .tex file
docs.text:
For each chapter, Claude wrote a first version. I opened the .tex file and wrote my own comments directly in it, where the change was needed. For example:

% Here I want an example.
% Here I want a figure.
% This figure is not correct.

Then I went back to the chat with Claude and said: "I put comments in the file, go through them."

I repeated this for several iterations, until I was happy with the chapter, then moved on to the next one.

docs.title: 5. One language first, then translate
docs.text: I worked on only one language. When a chapter was final in that language, I asked Claude to translate it into the other one (Catalan ↔ Spanish).

docs.title: 6. Publish
docs.text: The finished notes, in both languages, went on the course's page on the UB Campus Virtual.

docs.title: Result
docs.text: Complete lecture notes, in my style and following my slides and the pla docent, in both Catalan and Spanish, available to students on the Campus Virtual.

docs.title: What to watch for
docs.text:
• Template first. Settling the style before writing saves reformatting every chapter later.
  • Give structure and context. A LaTeX skeleton, the slides, the books and the pla docent all made the drafts closer to what I wanted.
  • Comments in the file work better than long chat messages. Each comment sits exactly where the change is needed.
  • Iterate per chapter. Finish one chapter before starting the next.
  • Finish one language before translating. Otherwise every correction has to be made twice.
  • Check the physics. Read every derivation and example: you remain responsible for the content.

docs.text:
New to Claude? Read these pages in order.

  1. How to get Claude: ask your group first, the Team plan for scientists if you are a PI
  2. Your first 30 minutes: what to do right after you get your account
  3. What Claude Pro includes: apps, models, features and usage limits

docs.title: Data and privacy
docs.text:
What happens to what you type and upload, and what you should keep out of Claude.

Not legal advice

This page summarises Anthropic's public policies as of October 2026. For anything that matters, check the Anthropic Privacy Center and the UB data protection rules.

docs.title: What happens to your data
docs.text:
Claude Pro is a consumer plan. Your chats are covered by Anthropic's Consumer Terms and Privacy Policy, not by a contract with UB.

Model training is your choice. The model improvement setting (Settings → Privacy, labelled Help Improve our AI models) decides whether your chats and Claude Code sessions can be used to train future models.

Setting Used for training? How long Anthropic keeps your chats Off (recommended) No Deleted chats are removed within 30 days On Yes Up to 5 years, in de-identified form

A few details:

  • Deleted chats are not used for future training, whatever the setting.
  • Incognito chats (an option when starting a new chat) are never used for training and do not appear in your history.
  • Thumbs up / down feedback sends that whole conversation to Anthropic, who may keep it for up to 5 years and use it for training, even with the setting off. Don't rate chats that contain sensitive material.
  • Chats flagged for safety review may be kept longer (up to 2 years).
  • Connectors (Google Drive, Gmail and so on) let Claude read what you point it to in that chat. That content is then part of the chat.
  • Folders on your computer that you open to Claude in the desktop app, Claude Code or Claude Science: what Claude reads from them is sent to Anthropic like an upload.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
Claude keeps a memory of useful context from your chats (your field, your courses, how you like answers), stored as separate topics. It is on by default on Pro.

  • See and edit it: Settings → Your Claude, then Manage next to Your memory. Open a topic to read, edit or delete it. You can also tell Claude in a chat to remember or forget something.
  • Turn it off: the Memory from chats toggle in the same place. Pausing keeps what is stored; resetting deletes it all.
  • One chat without memory: click + and switch off Memory before the first message, or use an incognito chat.
  • Projects have their own memory. To keep a Project completely separate from the rest, turn off Use account memory on the Project page.
  • Sensitive topics (health, politics, religion…) are not saved unless you turn on Include sensitive topics in memory. Leave it off.
  • Chat search: Claude can also search your past chats when it helps. Switch this off with Search and reference chats in Settings → Your Claude.

Memory is handy, but it also means something from one chat can show up in another. Turn it off for a chat about a confidential topic.

docs.title: What you can share
docs.text:
A simple rule: only upload what you would be comfortable emailing to a colleague outside UB. Then use the table below.

Material OK? Notes Published papers, public data, textbooks Yes Your own code and analysis scripts Yes Remove passwords, tokens and API keys first. Your own drafts and unpublished results Usually With training off. Check you are not bound by an embargo. Collaboration data and internal documents (Gaia, LSST, Euclid, LHCb, CTA…) Check first Many collaborations have their own AI or data-sharing rules. When in doubt, ask the collaboration. Referee reports and papers you are reviewing No Most journals forbid uploading manuscripts under review. Grant proposals you are evaluating No Evaluation is confidential; check the funder's rules. Student work, grades, emails with names No, unless anonymised Personal data falls under GDPR. Remove names and IDs. Personal data of anyone (CVs, health, HR) No Passwords, SSH keys, API tokens Never

docs.title: Good habits
docs.text:
1. Turn model improvement off in Settings → Privacy, unless you have a reason not to.
  2. Anonymise before you paste: replace names with Student A, remove email addresses and IDs.
  3. Use an incognito chat for one-off questions about something sensitive. It is not saved to your history or memory.
  4. Delete chats you no longer need.
  5. Credit AI use. Many journals ask you to state how AI was used. See Tips and pitfalls.

docs.title: When to use a local model instead
docs.text:
If the data cannot leave ICCUB at all, run an open model on your own machine or an ICCUB server. Nothing is sent to an outside company. The models are weaker than Claude, but often good enough for summarising, reformatting or code help.

  • Run a local LLM on your laptop
  • Share a local LLM over the network

docs.title: Your first 30 minutes
docs.text: You just got a Claude account: your own Pro plan or a seat on your group's Team plan (see How to get Claude). Here is what to do before your first real task. Each step takes a few minutes.

docs.title: 1. Sign in and check your plan
docs.text: Go to claude.ai and sign in with the email your account was created with. Open Settings → Billing (click your name, bottom left) and check that it says Pro (on a Team seat, your group's name appears instead). If it says Free, you are signed in with the wrong email.

docs.title: 2. Check your privacy settings
docs.text:
Open Settings → Privacy. The model improvement setting (labelled Help Improve our AI models) decides whether your chats can be used to train future models.

Recommended for ICCUB

Turn model improvement off if you will discuss unpublished results, collaboration data, referee reports or student work. Read Data and privacy before uploading anything sensitive.

docs.title: 3. Tell Claude who you are
docs.text:
Open Settings → Your Claude and fill in Instructions (in the older layout: Settings → Account → Instructions for Claude). These are short instructions Claude follows in every chat. For example:

I am an astrophysicist at the Institute of Cosmos Sciences (ICCUB),
University of Barcelona. I work mostly in Python and LaTeX.
Answer concisely, use SI or cgs units as appropriate, and say
clearly when you are unsure or when a reference should be checked.

You can change this at any time. In the same place you can see what Claude has saved in its memory about you (see Data and privacy).

docs.title: 4. Install the apps (optional)
docs.text:
The web version is enough to start. If you want more:

  • Desktop app for macOS and Windows, from claude.ai/download.
  • Mobile app for iOS and Android, from your app store. Your chats sync across all of them.
  • Claude Code, for working on code in your terminal or VS Code, is covered in Claude Code.
  • Claude in Chrome and the Microsoft 365 add-ins (Excel, Word, PowerPoint) put Claude in your browser and Office apps.

More detail in What Claude Pro includes.

docs.title: 5. Have a first conversation
docs.text:
Start a new chat and try something you actually need this week. A few ideas:

  • "Explain the difference between a Markov chain Monte Carlo and nested sampling, for a first-year PhD student."
  • Upload a paper PDF and ask: "Summarise the method and list the main assumptions."
  • Paste a Python function and ask: "Find bugs and suggest clearer variable names."
  • "Draft a short email to my students announcing that next week's class moves to room 503."

If the first answer is not right, reply and say what to change. Iterating in the same chat usually works better than starting over. See Chat and prompting.

docs.title: 6. Know the main controls
docs.text: Control Where What it does Model picker Below the message box Pick a model. Sonnet is fine for most work; Opus is slower but better at hard reasoning. Fable costs extra on Pro (see What Claude Pro includes). Effort Same menu How long Claude thinks before answering (older versions: Extended thinking). Raise it for derivations and tricky code. + button Left of the message box Upload files, start a Research report, switch connectors and memory on or off for this chat. Permission control In the message box Auto lets Claude work through a task without asking at each step; Manual makes it ask first. See Longer tasks. Projects Left sidebar Keep files and instructions together for one course or paper. See Projects.

docs.title: 7. Know the usage limits
docs.text: Pro has generous but finite usage. Long chats, large files, long tasks and Opus use your allowance faster. If you hit the limit, Claude tells you when it resets (usually within a few hours); Settings → Usage shows where you stand. Leave usage credits off unless you are willing to pay beyond the subscription. Starting a new chat for a new topic, instead of continuing a very long one, makes your allowance last longer.

docs.title: 8. Keep your judgement on
docs.text: Claude can be confidently wrong. Always check citations, numbers and derivations before you reuse them. Tips and pitfalls lists the common traps.

docs.title: How to get Claude
docs.text: Before you pay for anything, check whether you can join a plan that already exists.

docs.title: 1. Ask your group first
docs.text: Whether or not you are a PI, start by asking your colleagues and your PI whether the group already has Claude. Many groups have a Claude Team plan with free or spare seats, and your PI can add you in a few minutes. Ask before you buy a plan yourself.

docs.title: 2. If you are a PI: the Claude Team plan for scientists
docs.text:
Anthropic offers a Claude Team plan for scientists to principal investigators (or equivalent) at universities and non-profit research institutes, in the natural sciences, mathematics, computer science, engineering and related fields.

  1. Go to claude.com/programs/team-plan-for-scientists.
  2. Confirm your institutional affiliation (use your UB email) and briefly describe your research.
  3. Wait for the review. Most applications are reviewed within 5 to 7 working days; you get an email when you are approved.
  4. Once approved, add the members of your group as seats.

At the time of writing (October 2026), the Standard seat is free and the Premium seat (5× more usage) costs $15/month instead of $100, for the first 12 months, for up to 25 seats per group. Seats include Claude Code, Claude Science and the longer-task features. A group with no activity for 90 days may go back to normal Team pricing. Check the program page for the current conditions; promotional pricing is not guaranteed.

docs.title: 3. Otherwise: your own Pro plan
docs.text:
If no group plan is available to you, you can subscribe yourself to Claude Pro at claude.ai (Settings → Billing). See What Claude Pro includes and the official plan comparison.

Team plan or Pro: what changes

Most of this guide applies to both. A Team plan is a work account managed by your PI (the admin), with shared Projects and central billing, and it is covered by Anthropic's commercial terms rather than the consumer terms described in Data and privacy.

Got your account? Continue with Your first 30 minutes.

docs.title: What Claude Pro includes
docs.text:
What your Claude Pro account gives you, and when to use each part. Anthropic changes the details often; the official plan comparison is the reference.

Chat and Cowork are now one Claude

Since September 2026, what used to be a separate mode called Cowork (longer, multi-step tasks) is part of every conversation. You just describe what you need, and Claude either answers or works on the task for a while and hands you finished files. The change is rolling out gradually: if your message box still shows separate Chat and Cowork options, you don't have it yet. See Longer tasks and scheduling.

docs.title: Where you can use it
docs.text:
One account, the same chats everywhere:

Where Good for Web, at claude.ai Almost everything. Nothing to install. Desktop app (macOS, Windows), from claude.ai/download Same as web, plus access to folders on your computer, a built-in browser and the Code tab. Mobile app (iOS, Android) Quick questions, voice mode, photos of a blackboard, and following or steering long tasks you started at your desk. Claude Code (terminal, VS Code, JetBrains, desktop app, web) Working on your code and analysis scripts. See Claude Code. Claude in Chrome Claude reads and acts on web pages in your browser. See Claude in Chrome. Claude for Microsoft 365 Add-ins for Excel, Word and PowerPoint (Outlook in beta). See Email, calendar and documents. Claude Science (beta) A desktop workbench for running analyses with code, data and compute. See Claude Science.

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
Pick the model in the menu below the message box.

  • Sonnet is the everyday model. Fast and strong; use it for almost everything.
  • Opus is more capable. Use it for hard reasoning, long derivations or tricky code. It uses your allowance faster.
  • Haiku is the small, fast model, for quick simple tasks.
  • Fable is Anthropic's most advanced model. On Pro it is not covered by your plan's usage: it is paid separately with usage credits from the first message. Only pick it if you mean to pay for it.
  • Effort, in the same menu, sets how long Claude reasons before answering (older versions call it Extended thinking). The default suits most work; raise it for problems where you would want a colleague to think before replying, lower it for quick answers that use less of your allowance.

docs.text: Feature What it does More Chat and file upload Ask questions, upload PDFs, images, code, data files. Uploading files Projects Keep files and standing instructions together for one course, paper or proposal. Unlimited on Pro. Projects Artifacts: Docs, Slides, Design Claude writes documents, slide decks, designs and small interactive pages you can edit, export (Word, PDF, PowerPoint…) and share.
